title: Why did bigger chart summaries score worse on a shared cloud GPU — and how much can clinical rule checks recover?
summary: How much of a patient's medical record should we feed an AI at once? We tested five chart summary sizes — from a tiny 1k-token emergency snapshot up to a massive 128k-token multi-decade history — across four patients with records from multiple hospitals and clinics (48 runs total). All models ran on a standard shared 24 GB cloud GPU with a fixed 16,000-token active memory limit, comparing answers with and without Med Agent Hub's clinical rule checks, and were graded in a blinded review by two independent AI judges (Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4).
takeaway: Feeding a bigger chart to an AI backfires if the server's active memory window is smaller than the prompt. Scores peaked at the standard 8k summary, which fit comfortably inside the server's 16k memory limit: Gemma 4 26B with clinical rules led at 88.0/100 (8.75 accuracy, 9.12 completeness, zero unsafe answers), followed by Gemma 4 12B with clinical rules (80.5/100) and chart-only (80.2/100), while Qwen 3 14B scored 67.0/100. On the tight 1k summary, Med Agent Hub's clinical rule safety net beat chart-only by +19 points (43.8 vs. 24.8/100). When we sent 32k to 128k of chart text to that same 16k server, the server silently cut off the beginning of the prompt — erasing active allergies, current medications, and recent hospital stays — so chart-only scores collapsed to 0.0–2.8/100 (with 4/4 unsafe answers). Because Med Agent Hub attaches its pre-computed clinical conflict alerts at the very end of the prompt, those alerts survived the cutoff and rescued the medication conflict portion of the answer (27.0–32.8/100), though top-of-chart allergy checks remained cut off.
